nodes.title: Logic and Proof
nodes.essence: Mathematics is the subject in which statements are established by proof. This layer asks what a proof is, which arguments are valid, and what can be known about a system of axioms as a whole.

nodes.title: Formal Logic
nodes.essence: Formal logic makes mathematical reasoning itself an object of study. It fixes a precise language of formulas, says what it means for a formula to be true in a structure, and gives purely mechanical rules for deriving formulas from others.

nodes.title: Propositional Logic
nodes.essence: Propositional logic is the logic of "not", "and", "or", "if … then" and "if and only if", applied to statements treated as indivisible units that are either true or false.

nodes.title: Predicate Logic and Quantifiers
nodes.essence: Predicate logic, also called first-order logic, opens the atomic statements of propositional logic into statements about objects: predicates such as "x is prime", functions such as x + y, and the quantifiers ∀ ("for every") and ∃ ("there exists") which range over a domain.

nodes.title: Formal Proof Systems
nodes.essence: A formal proof system consists of axioms and rules of inference; a derivation is a finite list of formulas, each an axiom, a premise, or the result of a rule applied to earlier lines. Γ ⊢ φ means that a derivation of φ from premises in Γ exists, a purely syntactic fact.

nodes.title: Soundness, Completeness and Compactness
nodes.essence: Soundness says that a proof system derives only consequences: if Γ ⊢ φ then Γ ⊨ φ. Completeness says it derives all of them: if Γ ⊨ φ then Γ ⊢ φ, which Gödel proved for first-order logic in his doctoral thesis of 1929, published in 1930.

nodes.title: Methods of Proof
nodes.essence: This area is about how proofs are actually written: the small number of argument shapes that, combined, make up almost every proof in mathematics. A written proof is a compressed formal derivation, and its shape is dictated by the logical form of the statement.

nodes.title: What a Proof Is
nodes.essence: A proof is a finite argument that leads from accepted starting points (axioms, definitions and earlier theorems) to a conclusion by steps that any competent reader can check.

nodes.title: Direct Proof, Contraposition and Contradiction
nodes.essence: Most proofs of a statement P ⇒ Q take one of three shapes. A direct proof assumes P and reasons forward to Q. A proof by contraposition proves the equivalent statement ¬Q ⇒ ¬P. A proof by contradiction assumes the negation of what is to be proved and derives a contradiction.

nodes.title: Cases, Constructions and Counterexamples
nodes.essence: Three methods handle what direct proof leaves aside: disjunctions, existence, and universal claims that may be false. Proof by cases splits a problem into finitely many exhaustive possibilities and proves the claim in each.

nodes.title: Mathematical Induction
nodes.essence: Mathematical induction proves a statement P(n) for every natural number n from two finite pieces: the base case P(0) and the inductive step, that P(n) implies P(n + 1) for every n.

nodes.title: The Axiomatic Method
nodes.essence: The axiomatic method organises mathematics as theorems derived from explicitly stated axioms by explicitly stated logic. This area asks what such a system is, what can be known about it as a whole, and what changes when the logic itself is varied.

nodes.title: Axioms, Definitions and Theorems
nodes.essence: The axiomatic method organises a body of mathematics as a list of axioms, accepted without proof, from which every other statement is derived. Definitions add names for things built from the primitive notions, and theorems are what has been proved.

nodes.title: Consistency and Independence
nodes.essence: An axiom system is consistent if it does not prove a contradiction, and a statement is independent of it if the system proves neither the statement nor its negation. Both are established with models.

nodes.title: Constructive and Intuitionistic Logic
nodes.essence: Constructive mathematics requires that a proof of existence provide the object, and that a proof of "A or B" say which. Brouwer argued for this view from the early twentieth century; Heyting formalised its logic, intuitionistic logic, in 1930.

nodes.title: Sets and Foundations
nodes.essence: This layer supplies the language in which the rest of mathematics is written and the theory of infinite size. Its first area turns membership into sets, relations, functions and quotients: enough vocabulary to say what a group, a space or a probability is.

nodes.title: Sets, Relations and Functions
nodes.essence: This area supplies the vocabulary that the rest of mathematics is written in.

nodes.title: Sets and Set Operations
nodes.essence: A set is a collection treated as a single object, and it is determined entirely by its members: order, repetition and the way it was described carry no information.
keyTerms: A ∪ B, A ∩ B, A ∖ B

nodes.title: Relations and Orders
nodes.essence: A relation from A to B is a set of ordered pairs, a subset R ⊆ A × B, and "a R b" means (a, b) ∈ R. This turns any comparison (less than, divides, happens before) into an object with properties of its own.

nodes.title: Functions
nodes.essence: A function f: A → B assigns to each element of A exactly one element of B, and set theory makes that literal: f is a relation, a set of pairs, containing exactly one pair (a, b) for each a ∈ A.

nodes.title: Equivalence Relations and Quotients
nodes.essence: An equivalence relation declares things the same for a purpose: it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, like equality but coarser.

nodes.title: Infinity and Cardinality
nodes.essence: This area answers two questions that finite mathematics never has to separate: how many elements a set has, and how long a well-ordered list of them is. For finite sets the answers are the same number. For infinite sets they come apart, and both need new definitions.

nodes.title: Countable Sets
nodes.essence: Two sets have the same size when their elements can be matched one to one, which agrees with counting for finite sets and surprises for infinite ones. A set is countable when it can be listed as a sequence x₀, x₁, x₂, …, repeats allowed, or equivalently when it injects into ℕ.

nodes.title: Cantor's Diagonal Argument
nodes.essence: Given any list of objects of a certain kind, the diagonal argument builds a new object of that kind that differs from the n-th entry at the n-th place, so it is missing from the list.

nodes.title: Cardinal Numbers
nodes.essence: A cardinal number measures the size of a set, with no reference to order: two sets have the same cardinal when they are in bijection, and ∣A∣ ≤ ∣B∣ when A injects into B.

nodes.title: Ordinal Numbers and Transfinite Induction
nodes.essence: Cardinals measure how many; ordinals measure how long.

nodes.title: Axiomatic Set Theory
nodes.essence: The first two areas of this layer use sets freely. This area asks what justifies that use. Around 1900 the naive principle that every property defines a set turned out to be contradictory, and mathematicians responded by writing down exactly which sets exist.

nodes.title: Paradoxes and Naive Set Theory
nodes.essence: Naive set theory assumes that every property defines a set: for any condition P there is {x : P(x)}. That principle, unrestricted comprehension, is contradictory, and a two-line argument shows it.

nodes.title: Zermelo–Fraenkel Set Theory
nodes.essence: Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory (ZF) is a first-order theory with one relation symbol, ∈, and a short list of axioms saying which sets exist.

nodes.title: The Axiom of Choice
nodes.essence: The axiom of choice (AC) says that for any family of non-empty sets there is a function picking one element from each. For finitely many sets this is provable, and for sets with a rule for picking it is unnecessary; AC is needed only for infinitely many arbitrary choices.

nodes.title: Type Theory and Alternative Foundations
nodes.essence: Set theory is not the only possible foundation. A type theory gives every object a type when it is introduced, so a question such as "is x a member of itself?" cannot even be written down, and the paradoxes are blocked by grammar instead of by axioms.

nodes.title: Number Systems
nodes.essence: This layer is where the two roots of the knowledge base first produce the objects everyone uses. From logic it takes induction; from set theory it takes quotients, completions and the counting of infinite sets.

nodes.title: Constructing the Numbers
nodes.essence: This area builds the number systems instead of assuming them. It starts from the natural numbers, pinned down by Peano's axioms and modelled by von Neumann's sets, and climbs: ℤ and ℚ as quotients of pairs, ℝ by completing ℚ, ℂ as pairs of reals.

nodes.title: Natural Numbers and the Peano Axioms
nodes.essence: The natural numbers 0, 1, 2, … are what you reach from 0 by repeatedly taking "the next number", and nothing else.

nodes.title: Integers and Rational Numbers
nodes.essence: ℕ cannot solve 3 + x = 2 or 2 · x = 3. The integers and the rationals repair this without postulating anything new: an integer is a formal difference a − b, recorded as a pair (a, b) of naturals, and a rational is a formal quotient a/b, recorded as a pair of integers with b ≠ 0.

nodes.title: The Real Numbers
nodes.essence: ℚ is dense but full of holes: the rationals whose square is below 2 have no rational least upper bound. The real numbers fill every such hole.

nodes.title: The Complex Numbers
nodes.essence: ℝ has no square root of −1, so x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution. The complex numbers are pairs of reals, ℂ = ℝ², with (a, b) + (c, d) = (a + c, b + d) and (a, b)(c, d) = (ac − bd, ad + bc); writing i = (0, 1), every complex number is a + bi and i² = −1.

nodes.title: Algebraic and Transcendental Numbers
nodes.essence: A complex number is algebraic if it is a root of a non-zero polynomial with integer coefficients, as √2 is a root of x² − 2, and transcendental otherwise.

nodes.title: Extending Number Systems
nodes.essence: ℂ is algebraically closed, so polynomial equations give no reason to go further, but there are two other directions.

nodes.title: Elementary Number Theory
nodes.essence: Elementary number theory studies the integers using nothing beyond ℤ itself, induction and a little algebra: no complex analysis, no algebraic geometry. "Elementary" describes the tools, not the difficulty.

nodes.title: Divisibility and the Euclidean Algorithm
nodes.essence: In ℤ you cannot always divide, but you can always divide with a remainder, and that one fact drives elementary number theory.

nodes.title: Primes and Unique Factorisation
nodes.essence: A prime is an integer p > 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p. Every integer greater than 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from order: the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.

nodes.title: Modular Arithmetic
nodes.essence: Two integers are congruent modulo n when n divides their difference, a ≡ b (mod n). Congruence is an equivalence relation that respects addition and multiplication, so the n classes form a finite ring ℤ/n in which arithmetic is exact, like clock arithmetic.

nodes.title: Fermat, Euler and Primitive Roots
nodes.essence: The units modulo n form a finite group, and finiteness alone forces every unit to return to 1 when raised to a fixed power: Fermat's little theorem, aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p), and Euler's generalisation, a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n).

nodes.title: Quadratic Reciprocity
nodes.essence: Which numbers are perfect squares modulo a prime p? Half of the non-zero residues are, and Euler's criterion tests any one of them.

nodes.title: Diophantine Equations
nodes.essence: A Diophantine equation is a polynomial equation whose solutions are sought in integers or rationals, named after Diophantus of Alexandria.

nodes.title: Combinatorics and Graph Theory
nodes.essence: Combinatorics is the mathematics of finite structures: how many there are, how they are arranged, and which patterns they cannot avoid. Its objects are the simplest in mathematics, such as subsets, permutations, graphs and colourings.

nodes.title: Enumeration
nodes.essence: Enumeration answers "how many?" exactly. Its raw material is finite sets and bijections, and its basic move is to count the same set in two ways or to exhibit a bijection with a set already counted.

nodes.title: Counting Principles and Binomial Coefficients
nodes.essence: Counting answers "how many?" for a finite set without listing it.

nodes.title: Inclusion–Exclusion and the Pigeonhole Principle
nodes.essence: Two complementary tools for finite sets. Inclusion–exclusion computes the size of a union of overlapping sets from the sizes of their intersections, adding and subtracting in turn; it turns "count the objects with none of the bad properties" into a signed sum of easy counts.

nodes.title: Generating Functions
nodes.essence: A generating function encodes a sequence a₀, a₁, a₂, … as a formal power series A(x) = ∑ aₙxⁿ, so that operations on combinatorial objects become algebra on series: disjoint union becomes addition, pairing becomes multiplication, and a recursive description becomes an equation.

nodes.title: Recurrence Relations
nodes.essence: A recurrence relation defines each term of a sequence from earlier terms, as Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂ does for the Fibonacci numbers.

nodes.title: Combinatorial Sequences
nodes.essence: A handful of number sequences recur across combinatorics because the same few constructions recur: the Fibonacci numbers, the Catalan numbers, the Stirling and Bell numbers, and the partition numbers.

nodes.title: Graph Theory
nodes.essence: A graph records which pairs among a set of objects are connected, and nothing else. That austerity is its strength: the same theorems apply to road networks, molecules, schedules, electrical circuits and the internet.

nodes.title: Graphs and Connectivity
nodes.essence: A graph is a set of vertices together with a set of edges, each edge joining two vertices. It is the simplest mathematical model of anything made of pairwise connections: road maps, molecules, networks, dependencies, social ties.

nodes.title: Trees
nodes.essence: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles: just enough edges to hold the vertices together and not one more.

nodes.title: Matchings and Network Flows
nodes.essence: A matching pairs vertices along edges with no vertex used twice: workers with jobs, students with schools, rows with columns. A flow sends material from a source to a sink through a network of capacitated pipes.

nodes.title: Colouring and Planarity
nodes.essence: A proper colouring gives adjacent vertices different colours, and the chromatic number χ(G) is the fewest colours that suffice. Colouring models conflict avoidance: timetables, frequencies, registers. A planar graph is one that can be drawn in the plane without crossing edges.

nodes.title: Spectral Graph Theory and Expanders
nodes.essence: Spectral graph theory reads the structure of a graph from the eigenvalues of matrices attached to it, chiefly the adjacency matrix and the Laplacian.

nodes.title: Discrete Probability
nodes.essence: Probability on a finite or countable set is weighted counting. Every outcome gets a non-negative weight, the weights add up to 1, and the probability of an event is the total weight of its outcomes.

nodes.title: Finite Probability Spaces
nodes.essence: Probability on a finite or countable sample space is counting with weights. Each outcome ω in a set Ω gets a non-negative weight p(ω), the weights sum to 1, and the probability of an event, a subset of Ω, is the total weight of its outcomes.

nodes.title: Expectation and Variance
nodes.essence: A random variable is a numerical function of the outcome, and its expectation is its probability-weighted average.

nodes.title: The Probabilistic Method
nodes.essence: The probabilistic method proves that an object with some property exists by showing that a randomly chosen object has the property with positive probability. Nothing random is in the conclusion: in a finite space, positive probability means at least one outcome qualifies.

nodes.title: Random Graphs
nodes.essence: A random graph is built by deciding each possible edge by a coin toss.

nodes.title: Extremal Combinatorics
nodes.essence: Extremal combinatorics asks how large or how disordered a finite structure can be before some pattern is forced. How many vertices force a monochromatic clique in any two-colouring? How many edges force a triangle? How many subsets of an n-set can avoid containing one another?

nodes.title: Ramsey Theory
nodes.essence: Ramsey theory says that complete disorder is impossible: every sufficiently large structure, however it is coloured or split, contains a large orderly substructure. The model statement is about graphs.

nodes.title: Extremal Graph Theory
nodes.essence: Extremal graph theory asks how many edges a graph on n vertices can have without containing a given subgraph H. That maximum is the Turán number ex(n, H).

nodes.title: Posets and Extremal Set Theory
nodes.essence: A partially ordered set, or poset, is a set with a reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive order relation in which some pairs may be incomparable. Its two basic shapes are chains, in which every two elements are comparable, and antichains, in which no two are.

nodes.title: Additive Combinatorics
nodes.essence: Additive combinatorics studies the additive structure of sets: when a set of integers, or of elements of an abelian group, must contain arithmetic progressions, and what it means for a set to be nearly closed under addition. Its two central themes mirror each other.

nodes.title: Linear Algebra
nodes.essence: Linear algebra is the study of vector spaces and the linear maps between them.

nodes.title: Vector Spaces and Linear Maps
nodes.essence: This area builds the language of linear algebra from axioms. A vector space is any set where vectors can be added and scaled by elements of a field; a linear map is a function respecting those operations.

nodes.title: Fields and Vector Spaces
nodes.essence: A vector space is a set whose elements can be added and multiplied by scalars, subject to the familiar rules of arithmetic. The scalars come from a field, a number system in which one can add, subtract, multiply and divide by anything non-zero.

nodes.title: Linear Independence, Bases and Dimension
nodes.essence: A basis is a set of vectors from which every vector can be built in exactly one way. Choosing one turns abstract vectors into lists of numbers, their coordinates.

nodes.title: Linear Maps and Matrices
nodes.essence: A linear map is a function between vector spaces that respects addition and scalar multiplication: T(u + v) = Tu + Tv and T(av) = aTv. Once bases are chosen, every linear map between finite-dimensional spaces becomes a matrix, and composing maps becomes multiplying matrices.

nodes.title: Linear Systems and Rank–Nullity
nodes.essence: A system of m linear equations in n unknowns is a single equation Ax = b for an m × n matrix A.

nodes.title: Dual Spaces
nodes.essence: The dual space V∗ of a vector space V consists of the linear functionals, the linear maps V → F. A functional is a measurement: it takes a vector and returns a number, as a coordinate, a definite integral or an evaluation at a point does.

nodes.title: Determinants and Eigenvalues
nodes.essence: Rank classifies linear maps between two different spaces, but a map from a space to itself must be studied with one basis used on both sides, and then the classification is much richer. This area develops the invariants that survive such a change of basis.

nodes.title: Determinants
nodes.essence: The determinant assigns to each square matrix a single number that says by what factor the corresponding linear map scales volume, with a sign recording whether orientation is reversed.

nodes.title: Eigenvalues and Diagonalisation
nodes.essence: An eigenvector of a linear map T is a non-zero vector that T merely stretches: Tv = λv, and the stretch factor λ is the eigenvalue.

nodes.title: Jordan Normal Form
nodes.essence: Not every matrix can be diagonalised, but over an algebraically closed field such as ℂ every matrix is similar to one that is almost diagonal: eigenvalues on the diagonal, some ones just above it, zeros everywhere else.

nodes.title: Non-negative Matrices and Perron–Frobenius
nodes.essence: A matrix with no negative entries models anything that flows, grows or moves without cancellation: probabilities passing between states, populations passing between age classes, links passing importance between web pages.

nodes.title: Inner Product Spaces
nodes.essence: A bare vector space has no lengths or angles. An inner product supplies them, and with them come perpendicularity, orthonormal bases, projections and the adjoint of a map. This extra structure changes what can be proved.

nodes.title: Inner Products and Orthogonality
nodes.essence: An inner product adds geometry to a vector space: lengths, angles and, above all, perpendicularity. The dot product on ℝⁿ is the model, but the same axioms apply to functions, where the inner product is an integral, and to random variables, where it is a covariance.

nodes.title: The Spectral Theorem
nodes.essence: The spectral theorem says that the matrices compatible with an inner product are exactly as simple as one could hope.

nodes.title: Singular Value Decomposition
nodes.essence: The Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) writes every matrix, square or not, as a rotation, a scaling along perpendicular axes, and another rotation: A = UΣVᵀ.

nodes.title: Quadratic Forms and Positive Definiteness
nodes.essence: A quadratic form is a homogeneous polynomial of degree two, such as q(x, y) = x² + 4xy + y², or in matrix language q(x) = xᵀAx with A symmetric.

nodes.title: Multilinear Algebra
nodes.essence: Linear algebra studies maps that are linear in one variable. Many of the most important constructions are linear in several variables separately: the inner product, the determinant, matrix multiplication, the curvature of a surface.

nodes.title: Tensor Products
nodes.essence: The tensor product V ⊗ W is the space that turns bilinear maps into linear ones.

nodes.title: Exterior Algebra
nodes.essence: The exterior algebra of a vector space is the algebra of oriented areas, volumes and their higher analogues. Its product, the wedge product, is anticommutative: v ∧ w = −w ∧ v, so v ∧ v = 0.

nodes.title: Abstract Algebra
nodes.essence: Abstract algebra asks what structure alone implies. It takes the operations that appear across mathematics, such as composing symmetries, adding and multiplying numbers or polynomials, and applying linear maps.

nodes.title: Groups
nodes.essence: A group is the algebra of reversible operations: one associative operation, an identity and inverses.

nodes.title: Groups and Subgroups
nodes.essence: A group is a set with one associative operation, an identity element and inverses: the least structure in which every action can be undone. The symmetries of any object form a group, because symmetries compose, "do nothing" is a symmetry, and each one can be reversed.

nodes.title: Homomorphisms and Quotient Groups
nodes.essence: A homomorphism is a map between groups that respects the operation; it is how groups are compared. Its kernel, the set of elements sent to the identity, records exactly what the map forgets.

nodes.title: Group Actions
nodes.essence: Groups matter because they act: an action lets each element of a group G move the points of a set X, compatibly with the group law.

nodes.title: The Sylow Theorems
nodes.essence: Lagrange's theorem says that subgroup orders divide the group order, and its converse is false. Sylow showed in 1872 that the converse does hold for the largest power of each prime, and with remarkable control.

nodes.title: Composition Series and Simple Groups
nodes.essence: As integers factor into primes, finite groups break into simple groups, those with no normal subgroups except the trivial one and themselves.

nodes.title: Free Groups and Presentations
nodes.essence: The free group on a set S is the group of reduced words in the letters of S and their inverses: the group with no relations at all.

nodes.title: Rings and Fields
nodes.essence: Groups have one operation; most of arithmetic has two. A ring adds and multiplies, as ℤ, polynomials and matrices do, and a field also divides, as ℚ, ℝ, ℂ and ℤ/p do.

nodes.title: Rings and Ideals
nodes.essence: A ring is a set where you can add, subtract and multiply, as in ℤ, polynomials or matrices.

nodes.title: Factorisation in Integral Domains
nodes.essence: Unique factorisation into primes feels like a law of nature, but it is a property of particular rings.

nodes.title: Polynomial Rings
nodes.essence: A polynomial over a ring R is a formal expression a₀ + a₁x + ⋯ + aₙxⁿ, a finite list of coefficients, not a function. Over a field F the ring F[x] behaves like ℤ: it has division with remainder, greatest common divisors and unique factorisation into irreducible polynomials.

nodes.title: Field Extensions
nodes.essence: A field extension L/K is a field L containing a smaller field K, such as ℚ ⊂ ℚ(√2) ⊂ ℝ ⊂ ℂ. The decisive observation is that L is a vector space over K, so linear algebra applies: the degree [L : K] is its dimension, and degrees multiply along towers.

nodes.title: Finite Fields
nodes.essence: Finite fields are completely classified, and the classification is short. A field with q elements exists if and only if q is a prime power pⁿ, and it is unique up to isomorphism, so one can speak of the field 𝔽_q.

nodes.title: Commutative Rings and Localisation
nodes.essence: Commutative algebra treats a ring as a space and its elements as functions on it. The points are the prime ideals, forming the prime spectrum Spec R, and f "vanishes" at P when f ∈ P.

nodes.title: Galois Theory
nodes.essence: Galois theory attaches a finite group to a field extension, the group of symmetries of the roots of a polynomial that respect every algebraic relation among them, and shows that the group knows everything about the fields in between.

nodes.title: The Galois Correspondence
nodes.essence: The Galois group of a field extension L/K is the group of automorphisms of L that fix every element of K; for a splitting field it permutes the roots of the polynomial while preserving every algebraic relation among them.

nodes.title: Solvability by Radicals
nodes.essence: A polynomial is solvable by radicals when its roots can be written from its coefficients using only addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and n-th roots. Quadratics, cubics and quartics always are; the formulas for degrees 3 and 4 were published by Cardano in 1545.

nodes.title: Ruler-and-Compass Constructions
nodes.essence: Greek geometers asked for constructions using only an unmarked straightedge and a compass, and left three problems unsolved: doubling the cube, trisecting an arbitrary angle and squaring the circle. For two thousand years nobody could do them or prove they were impossible.

nodes.title: Modules and Representations
nodes.essence: Linear algebra is the best-understood part of mathematics, and this area extends its reach in two directions. Modules keep the vector space axioms but let the scalars come from a ring.

nodes.title: Modules
nodes.essence: A module is a vector space whose scalars come from a ring instead of a field. The definition is the same, but the consequences differ: without division, modules need not have bases, and elements can be killed by non-zero scalars. The concept unifies three familiar objects.

nodes.title: Representations of Finite Groups
nodes.essence: A representation of a group G is a way for G to act by invertible linear maps on a vector space: a homomorphism ρ from G to the group GL(V) of invertible linear maps. It turns abstract symmetry into matrices, where linear algebra can work on it.

nodes.title: Real Analysis
nodes.essence: Calculus was invented in the seventeenth century and used with spectacular success for nearly two hundred years before anyone could say exactly what a derivative or an integral was. Real analysis is the rigorous version.

nodes.title: Limits and Convergence
nodes.essence: How can a process that never ends have a definite outcome? The decimal 0.999… equals 1, the sum 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ⋯ equals 1, and a curve can have an exact slope at a point, yet each involves infinitely many steps. The answer, made precise in the nineteenth century, is the limit.

nodes.title: Sequences and Limits
nodes.essence: A sequence is a function from ℕ to ℝ, written a₁, a₂, a₃, …. Saying that aₙ tends to L means: for every tolerance ε > 0 there is a stage N after which every term lies within ε of L.

nodes.title: Series
nodes.essence: A series a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + ⋯ is not an infinite addition. It is the limit of its partial sums sₙ = a₁ + ⋯ + aₙ, and it converges when that limit exists.

nodes.title: Continuity
nodes.essence: A function f from a set D ⊆ ℝ to ℝ is continuous at a point a when small changes of input give small changes of output: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that |x − a| < δ implies |f(x) − f(a)| < ε. Equivalently, f preserves limits: xₙ → a implies f(xₙ) → f(a).

nodes.title: Uniform Convergence
nodes.essence: A sequence of functions fₙ can converge to f in two very different ways. Pointwise: for each x separately, fₙ(x) → f(x). Uniformly: the worst error over all x, sup |fₙ(x) − f(x)|, tends to 0, so one stage N works for every x at once.

nodes.title: Estimates and Inequalities
nodes.essence: Analysis proves that things are equal, or that limits exist, by proving inequalities. To show aₙ → L you rarely compute aₙ − L; you bound it. A handful of inequalities do almost all the work, and each has a one-line reason.

nodes.title: Calculus of One Variable
nodes.essence: Newton and Leibniz built calculus in the seventeenth century as a set of extraordinarily effective rules, justified by infinitesimals nobody could define. This area rebuilds those rules on the limit.

nodes.title: The Derivative and the Mean Value Theorem
nodes.essence: The derivative of f at a is the slope of the best linear approximation to f near a: f(a + h) = f(a) + f′(a)h + o(h), where o(h) stands for an error that is small even compared with h.

nodes.title: Taylor Expansion
nodes.essence: The derivative gives the best linear approximation to a function; Taylor expansion gives the best polynomial approximation of each degree.

nodes.title: The Riemann Integral
nodes.essence: The integral of f over [a, b] is meant to be the signed area under its graph.

nodes.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
nodes.essence: Differentiation measures local change; integration adds up accumulated change. The fundamental theorem of calculus (FTC) says they undo each other. Part 1: integrating a continuous f from a to x gives a function whose derivative is f.

nodes.title: The Exponential and Trigonometric Functions
nodes.essence: School mathematics defines powers by roots and sin and cos by triangles, then assumes their derivatives. Analysis reverses the order.

nodes.title: Power Series and Analytic Functions
nodes.essence: A power series ∑cₙ(x − a)ⁿ is a polynomial of infinite degree, and inside its radius of convergence it behaves like one: it can be added, multiplied and differentiated term by term, and its coefficients are its derivatives at a divided by n!.

nodes.title: Metric Spaces
nodes.essence: The theorems of one-variable analysis seem to be about numbers, but their proofs use very little of ℝ: a distance, the triangle inequality, completeness, and the fact that closed bounded intervals trap sequences. This area isolates those ingredients.

nodes.title: Metric Spaces and Continuity
nodes.essence: The proofs about limits and continuity in ℝ use almost nothing but the distance |x − y| and the triangle inequality. A metric space keeps exactly that: a set with a distance function obeying three axioms.

nodes.title: Completeness and the Contraction Mapping Principle
nodes.essence: A metric space is complete when every sequence whose terms bunch together, a Cauchy sequence, actually converges to a point of the space. ℝ is complete and ℚ is not, and the same contrast appears in every corner of analysis: completeness is what lets a proof say "the limit exists" without naming it.

nodes.title: Compactness in Metric Spaces
nodes.essence: A compact space is one in which infinite processes cannot escape: every sequence has a convergent subsequence, and every covering by open sets can be cut down to finitely many.

nodes.title: Calculus of Several Variables
nodes.essence: Most quantities depend on more than one variable, so calculus has to work in ℝⁿ. The step from one variable to several is not just more of the same. The derivative stops being a number and becomes a linear map, so linear algebra becomes part of calculus.

nodes.title: The Derivative as a Linear Map
nodes.essence: In one variable the derivative looks like a number, the slope. In several variables it must be what that number always secretly was: the linear map that best approximates the change in f near a point.

nodes.title: Inverse and Implicit Function Theorems
nodes.essence: Linear algebra says exactly when a linear system can be solved and how many free parameters the solutions have.

nodes.title: Extrema and Lagrange Multipliers
nodes.essence: Finding the largest or smallest value of a function of several variables takes three separate steps. First, show that an extremum exists, usually by compactness.

nodes.title: Multiple Integrals and Change of Variables
nodes.essence: The integral of a function over a region of ℝⁿ is defined exactly as in one variable, by squeezing between upper and lower sums, now over grids of small boxes. Two theorems make it computable.

nodes.title: Vector Calculus and the Integral Theorems
nodes.essence: The fundamental theorem of calculus says that integrating a derivative over an interval gives the values at its two endpoints. Vector calculus finds the same pattern one dimension up, twice more.

nodes.title: Topology
nodes.essence: Topology is the study of the properties of a space that survive continuous deformation: stretching, bending and squeezing, but not tearing or gluing.

nodes.title: Point-Set Topology
nodes.essence: Real analysis showed that continuity, convergence and compactness can be phrased entirely through open sets of a metric space, without mentioning distances. Point-set topology takes that observation as a definition.

nodes.title: Topological Spaces and Continuous Maps
nodes.essence: A topological space is a set together with a chosen family of "open" sets, closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections.

nodes.title: Subspaces, Products and Quotients
nodes.essence: New spaces are made from old ones in three ways: by restricting to a subset, by multiplying spaces, and by gluing points together.

nodes.title: Compactness
nodes.essence: A space is compact if every cover of it by open sets has a finite subcover.

nodes.title: Connectedness
nodes.essence: A space is connected if it cannot be split into two disjoint non-empty open sets.

nodes.title: Separation Axioms and Metrisability
nodes.essence: The axioms of a topology alone allow spaces in which a sequence converges to two limits or a point cannot be told apart from a closed set.

nodes.title: Algebraic Topology
nodes.essence: How do you prove that two spaces are not homeomorphic, or that a map with some property cannot exist? Point-set invariants such as compactness and connectedness are too coarse: they cannot tell a sphere from a torus.

nodes.title: Homotopy and the Fundamental Group
nodes.essence: Two loops in a space are homotopic if one can be deformed continuously into the other, and the homotopy classes of loops at a base point form a group, the fundamental group π₁, under "go round one loop, then the other".

nodes.title: Covering Spaces
nodes.essence: A covering map p: E → X looks, over each small open set of X, like a stack of disjoint copies of that set; the real line wrapping round the circle is the model.

nodes.title: Homology
nodes.essence: Homology counts holes of each dimension by linear algebra. A space is broken into simplices (points, edges, triangles, tetrahedra and their higher analogues); formal sums of n-simplices are n-chains, and the boundary map ∂ sends each simplex to the signed sum of its faces.

nodes.title: The Euler Characteristic
nodes.essence: For any convex polyhedron, vertices minus edges plus faces equals 2: a cube has 8 − 12 + 6 = 2, a tetrahedron 4 − 6 + 4 = 2. Euler noticed this; topology explains it.

nodes.title: Fixed-Point Theorems
nodes.essence: Stir a cup of coffee and let it settle: some point of the liquid ends where it started. This is an instance of Brouwer's fixed-point theorem: every continuous map from a closed disc (or ball) to itself fixes a point.

nodes.title: Higher Homotopy Groups and Fibrations
nodes.essence: The fundamental group records loops, maps of a circle into a space; the n-th homotopy group πₙ records maps of the n-sphere, up to deformation.

nodes.title: Cohomology and Poincaré Duality
nodes.essence: Cohomology is homology seen through its dual: instead of chains, one studies functions on chains, and every arrow reverses.

nodes.title: Manifolds
nodes.essence: Manifolds are the spaces that look like ordinary ℝⁿ near every point: curves, surfaces, the 3-dimensional universe, configuration spaces of machines, groups of rotations.

nodes.title: Topological and Smooth Manifolds
nodes.essence: A manifold is a space that looks like ordinary ℝⁿ near each of its points, however twisted it is globally. The Earth's surface is the model: every atlas page is a flat map of a small region, and the pages overlap consistently, yet no single flat page shows the whole sphere.

nodes.title: Classification of Surfaces
nodes.essence: Classification is the dream of every area of mathematics: a complete list of the objects, and a way to tell which one you are holding. For closed surfaces the dream comes true.

nodes.title: Knot Theory
nodes.essence: A knot is a closed loop of string in space with the ends fused, and two knots are the same if one can be moved into the other without cutting.

nodes.title: Three-Manifolds and the Poincaré Conjecture
nodes.essence: Is a closed 3-dimensional space in which every loop can be shrunk to a point necessarily the 3-sphere? Poincaré asked this in 1904, and it became the most famous problem in topology.

nodes.title: Geometry
nodes.essence: Geometry is the study of shape, size and symmetry, and of what stays the same when a space is moved, bent or projected.

nodes.title: Classical Geometry
nodes.essence: Classical geometry is the story of how geometry stopped being a single body of truths about space and became a family of theories.

nodes.title: Euclidean Geometry
nodes.essence: Euclid's Elements, written in Alexandria about 2,300 years ago, derives plane geometry from five postulates, and the fifth, the parallel postulate, never looked as obvious as the rest.

nodes.title: Non-Euclidean Geometry
nodes.essence: For centuries geometers assumed the negation of the parallel postulate and hunted for a contradiction.

nodes.title: Projective Geometry
nodes.essence: Projective geometry began with Renaissance perspective, which keeps straight lines and incidences but changes lengths, angles and parallelism. Made precise, it is the geometry of lines through the origin of a vector space.

nodes.title: Symmetry Groups and Tilings
nodes.essence: The symmetries of a pattern are the rigid motions that map it onto itself, and they always form a group.

nodes.title: The Erlangen Programme
nodes.essence: By 1870 there were many geometries, Euclidean, hyperbolic, spherical, affine and projective, and no clear account of how they related.

nodes.title: Differential Geometry
nodes.essence: Differential geometry uses calculus to measure shape. Its central quantity is curvature: how a curve bends, how a surface departs from its tangent plane, how parallel transport around a loop fails to return a vector to itself.

nodes.title: Curves and Curvature
nodes.essence: Differential geometry begins by asking how a curve bends. Parametrised by arc length, a curve has a unit tangent, and the rate at which that tangent turns is the curvature, the reciprocal of the radius of the best-fitting circle.

nodes.title: Surfaces and Gaussian Curvature
nodes.essence: A surface in space bends differently in different directions, and two quadratic forms record how: the first measures lengths on the surface, the second measures how the surface curves away from its tangent plane.

nodes.title: The Gauss–Bonnet Theorem
nodes.essence: Gaussian curvature changes when a surface is dented, but the Gauss–Bonnet theorem says its total over a closed surface never does: it always equals 2π times the Euler characteristic. A sphere, however lumpy, has total curvature 4π; a torus, however twisted, has total curvature 0.

nodes.title: Differential Forms and de Rham Cohomology
nodes.essence: Differential forms are the things that can be integrated over curves, surfaces and their higher-dimensional analogues, independently of coordinates.

nodes.title: Riemannian Manifolds
nodes.essence: Riemann's 1854 lecture on the hypotheses underlying geometry took Gauss's intrinsic view of surfaces and made it the definition of geometry in any dimension: a smooth manifold with an inner product on each tangent space, varying smoothly.

nodes.title: Vector Bundles, Connections and Characteristic Classes
nodes.essence: A vector bundle attaches a vector space to each point of a manifold, varying smoothly and looking like a product over small regions, but possibly twisted globally, as the Möbius band twists a line around a circle.

nodes.title: Symplectic Geometry
nodes.essence: Riemannian geometry measures lengths with a symmetric form; symplectic geometry measures oriented areas with an antisymmetric one.

nodes.title: Convex and Discrete Geometry
nodes.essence: Convex and discrete geometry studies shapes defined by finitely many pieces of linear data: half-spaces, vertices, lattice points.

nodes.title: Convex Sets and Separation
nodes.essence: A set is convex when it contains the segment between any two of its points. That single condition gives convex sets a property arbitrary sets lack: any point outside a closed convex set can be cut off from it by a hyperplane.

nodes.title: Polytopes
nodes.essence: A convex polytope is the convex hull of finitely many points, or equivalently a bounded intersection of finitely many half-spaces.

nodes.title: Lattices and Sphere Packing
nodes.essence: A lattice is a discrete grid in ℝⁿ, all integer combinations of a basis, and the sphere-packing problem asks how densely equal balls can fill space.

nodes.title: Lie Theory
nodes.essence: Lie theory studies continuous symmetry. The rotations of space, the unitary transformations of quantum states and the Lorentz transformations of relativity are not finite groups but smooth families, groups that are also manifolds.

nodes.title: Lie Groups and Lie Algebras
nodes.essence: A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold, with smooth multiplication and inversion: the rotations SO(3), the unitary matrices U(n), the Lorentz group.

nodes.title: The Classification of Simple Lie Algebras
nodes.essence: A simple Lie algebra has no ideals except zero and itself, and is not abelian; every semisimple algebra is a direct sum of simple ones.

nodes.title: Representations of Lie Groups
nodes.essence: A representation of a Lie group G is a smooth homomorphism from G to the invertible linear maps of a vector space: a way for the group to act linearly. Representations are how symmetry is used in practice, because linear actions can be decomposed, measured by traces and compared.

nodes.title: Advanced Analysis
nodes.essence: This layer asks how we measure, integrate and decompose in infinite dimensions. Real analysis in layer 06 handles one function at a time: its limits, derivatives and Riemann integral.

nodes.title: Measure and Integration
nodes.essence: The Riemann integral of layer 06 works for continuous functions on intervals, but it breaks under limits: a pointwise limit of integrable functions need not be integrable, and the space of Riemann integrable functions is not complete. Measure theory repairs this at the root.

nodes.title: Measure and σ-Algebras
nodes.essence: A measure assigns a size (length, area, probability) to sets and is countably additive: the size of a countable disjoint union is the sum of the sizes. The Riemann integral handles only sets that finitely many boxes approximate well.

nodes.title: The Lebesgue Integral
nodes.essence: Riemann slices the domain into intervals; Henri Lebesgue, in his thesis of 1902, sliced the range instead and asked how large the set is where the function takes values in each slice.

nodes.title: Lᵖ Spaces
nodes.essence: For 1 ≤ p < ∞, the space Lᵖ(μ) consists of the measurable functions f with ∫ ∣f∣ᵖ dμ < ∞, measured by the norm ‖f‖ₚ = (∫ ∣f∣ᵖ dμ)^(1/p); L^∞ consists of the functions bounded outside a null set.

nodes.title: The Radon–Nikodym Theorem
nodes.essence: Given two measures μ and ν on the same σ-algebra, when is ν given by a density, ν(A) = ∫ over A of f dμ? An obvious necessary condition is that every μ-null set is ν-null. The Radon–Nikodym theorem says this condition is also sufficient, provided both measures are σ-finite.

nodes.title: Hausdorff Dimension and Fractals
nodes.essence: Length, area and volume suit sets of dimension 1, 2 and 3 and fail on others: a square has infinite length and zero volume. Felix Hausdorff (1918) defined a measure Hˢ for every real s ≥ 0 by covering a set with small pieces and adding up (diameter)ˢ.

nodes.title: Complex Analysis
nodes.essence: Complex analysis is calculus with complex numbers, and it behaves nothing like its real counterpart.

nodes.title: Holomorphic Functions
nodes.essence: A function f of a complex variable is holomorphic on an open set if the limit f′(z) = lim (f(z + h) − f(z))/h exists at every point, with h → 0 through complex values.

nodes.title: Cauchy's Theorem and Its Consequences
nodes.essence: Cauchy's theorem says that the integral of a holomorphic function around a closed curve is 0, provided the curve can be shrunk to a point without leaving the domain.

nodes.title: Singularities and Residues
nodes.essence: A holomorphic function on a punctured disc around z₀ has an isolated singularity at z₀. Its behaviour there falls into exactly three types, read off from a Laurent series, a power series that is allowed negative powers.

nodes.title: Conformal Maps and the Riemann Mapping Theorem
nodes.essence: A holomorphic function with non-zero derivative preserves angles, so it is a conformal map: it distorts sizes but keeps the shape of infinitesimal figures. Conformal maps between plane regions are surprisingly plentiful and surprisingly rigid at once.

nodes.title: Analytic Continuation and Riemann Surfaces
nodes.essence: Because a holomorphic function is determined by its values on any small disc, a power series converging near one point can have at most one holomorphic extension along a given path.

nodes.title: Functional Analysis
nodes.essence: Functional analysis is linear algebra in infinite dimensions, made workable by analysis. Its objects are spaces of functions, such as the continuous functions on an interval or the square-integrable functions on a domain, treated as single points in a vector space with a norm.

nodes.title: Banach Spaces
nodes.essence: A Banach space is a vector space with a norm, a notion of length, in which every Cauchy sequence converges.

nodes.title: Hilbert Spaces
nodes.essence: A Hilbert space is a Banach space whose norm comes from an inner product ⟨x, y⟩, so that lengths and angles both make sense.

nodes.title: Hahn–Banach and Baire Category
nodes.essence: Four theorems carry most of the weight of functional analysis. The Hahn–Banach theorem says there are enough continuous linear functionals: any functional on a subspace extends to the whole space without growing, and convex sets can be separated by hyperplanes.

nodes.title: Spectral Theory
nodes.essence: In finite dimensions a symmetric matrix is diagonal in an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, and its eigenvalues are the numbers λ for which A − λ fails to be invertible. Spectral theory carries this to operators on infinite-dimensional spaces.

nodes.title: Compact Operators and Fredholm Theory
nodes.essence: Ivar Fredholm's 1903 paper on integral equations f(x) − ∫ k(x, y)·f(y) dy = g(x) found that they behave like square linear systems: either there is exactly one solution for every g, or the homogeneous equation has solutions, and then g must satisfy finitely many conditions.

nodes.title: Harmonic Analysis
nodes.essence: Harmonic analysis decomposes functions into oscillations. A sound is a sum of pitches, a periodic temperature profile a sum of sine waves, an image a sum of spatial frequencies.

nodes.title: Fourier Series
nodes.essence: A Fourier series writes a periodic function as a sum of pure oscillations, f(x) ~ ∑ f̂(n)·e^(inx), with coefficients f̂(n) = (1/2π)·∫ f(x)·e^(−inx) dx over one period.

nodes.title: The Fourier Transform
nodes.essence: The Fourier transform is the Fourier series of a function on the whole line, where frequencies form a continuum instead of the integers.

nodes.title: Distributions
nodes.essence: Physicists and engineers used the Dirac delta, a "function" that is zero except at one point yet has integral 1, long before anyone could say what it was.

nodes.title: Fourier Analysis on Groups
nodes.essence: Fourier series live on the circle and the Fourier transform on the line, but what makes both work is only that the circle and the line are groups. The exponentials e^(inx) and e^(2πixξ) are characters: continuous homomorphisms into the unit circle.

nodes.title: Differential Equations and Dynamics
nodes.essence: This layer asks how laws of change determine the future. Since Newton, the laws of science have mostly been written as differential equations: a rule giving the rate of change of a state in terms of the state itself. Knowing the law is only the start.

nodes.title: Ordinary Differential Equations
nodes.essence: An ordinary differential equation (ODE) prescribes how a state changes in time: y′ = f(t, y), with y a point of ℝⁿ. Newton's laws, chemical kinetics, population models and electrical circuits all take this form.

nodes.title: Existence and Uniqueness
nodes.essence: An ordinary differential equation (ODE) y′ = f(t, y) prescribes the velocity of a state y ∈ ℝⁿ at each time t; with a starting value y(t₀) = y₀ it becomes an initial value problem (IVP). Does this law of change determine one future, and only one?

nodes.title: Linear Systems and the Matrix Exponential
nodes.essence: The linear system x′ = Ax, with x ∈ ℝⁿ and A a constant n × n matrix, is the one large class of differential equations solved completely: x(t) = e^(tA)·x(0), where the matrix exponential e^(tA) = I + tA + t²A²/2! + … is the same series as eᵗ.

nodes.title: Stability and Phase Portraits
nodes.essence: Most nonlinear systems x′ = f(x) have no solution formula, so one asks qualitative questions instead: where are the equilibria, which are stable, and what does the flow look like as a whole? A phase portrait answers by drawing the trajectories in state space.

nodes.title: Boundary Value Problems and Sturm–Liouville Theory
nodes.essence: A boundary value problem (BVP) asks for a solution of a differential equation that meets conditions at both ends of an interval, like a string fixed at both ends.

nodes.title: Partial Differential Equations
nodes.essence: A partial differential equation (PDE) relates an unknown function of several variables, such as position and time, to its partial derivatives.

nodes.title: First-Order Equations and Characteristics
nodes.essence: A first-order partial differential equation (PDE) relates a function u of several variables to its first partial derivatives. The model is the transport equation uₜ + c·uₓ = 0, which says that the profile of u is carried along at speed c.

nodes.title: Laplace's Equation and Harmonic Functions
nodes.essence: Laplace's equation Δu = 0, where the Laplacian Δu = ∂²u/∂x₁² + … + ∂²u/∂xₙ², describes every steady state of diffusion: equilibrium temperature, electrostatic potential away from charges, the velocity potential of an ideal fluid.

nodes.title: The Heat Equation
nodes.essence: The heat equation uₜ = Δu says that the temperature at a point rises at a rate proportional to how far it lies below the average of its neighbours.

nodes.title: The Wave Equation
nodes.essence: The wave equation uₜₜ = c²Δu governs vibrating strings, sound, light and small ripples on water.

nodes.title: Weak Solutions and Sobolev Spaces
nodes.essence: Looking directly for twice-differentiable solutions of a partial differential equation (PDE) usually fails: the natural spaces of smooth functions are not complete for the right norms, and the solutions often are not smooth. The modern method splits the problem in two.

nodes.title: Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
nodes.essence: Nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) describe fluids, gravity, chemical reactions and biological patterns, and there is no general theory of them.

nodes.title: Calculus of Variations
nodes.essence: The calculus of variations optimises over functions instead of numbers.

nodes.title: The Euler–Lagrange Equation
nodes.essence: The calculus of variations looks for functions that make an integral as small as possible, or at least stationary: shortest paths, the curve of fastest descent, soap films, the motion of planets.

nodes.title: Noether's Theorem
nodes.essence: Emmy Noether's theorem (1918) says that each continuous symmetry of the action of a variational problem yields a quantity conserved along every solution.

nodes.title: Existence of Minimisers
nodes.essence: The Euler–Lagrange equation says what a minimiser must satisfy if there is one; whether there is one is a separate question. The nineteenth century learned this the hard way.

nodes.title: Dynamical Systems
nodes.essence: A dynamical system is a rule for how a state evolves: a map applied repeatedly, xₙ₊₁ = f(xₙ), or the flow of a differential equation. Dynamical systems theory gives up on formulas for individual solutions and asks about long-term behaviour. Where do orbits end up?

nodes.title: Iterated Maps
nodes.essence: Iterating a map, xₙ₊₁ = f(xₙ), is the simplest dynamical system: time moves in steps, as in yearly population counts, Newton's method, or the successive crossings of a flow through a surface. One dimension already holds almost every phenomenon of dynamics.

nodes.title: Bifurcations
nodes.essence: A bifurcation is a qualitative change in a system's behaviour as a parameter passes a critical value: equilibria appear or vanish, exchange stability, or give way to oscillation.

nodes.title: Chaos and Strange Attractors
nodes.essence: A deterministic system is chaotic when tiny differences in the starting state grow exponentially, so long-term prediction is impossible in practice even though the future is fixed in principle.

nodes.title: Ergodic Theory
nodes.essence: Ergodic theory studies dynamical systems that preserve a measure, and asks when following one orbit for a long time is the same as averaging over the whole space.

nodes.title: Hamiltonian Systems and Integrability
nodes.essence: Hamiltonian systems are the dynamics of mechanics without friction: planets, particles, light rays and, through quantisation, atoms. Their flows preserve a geometric structure, the symplectic form, which forbids attractors and makes phase-space volume constant.

nodes.title: Complex Dynamics
nodes.essence: Iterate a polynomial such as z ↦ z² + c on the complex plane. Most starting points settle into regular behaviour or escape to infinity, and the boundary between the two, the Julia set, is usually a fractal on which the map is chaotic.

nodes.title: Probability and Statistics
nodes.essence: This layer makes chance rigorous and then turns it around to learn from data. Probability began with games: Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat solved the problem of dividing the stakes of an interrupted game in their correspondence of 1654.

nodes.title: Measure-Theoretic Probability
nodes.essence: Finite probability counts: the probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of its outcomes. That breaks as soon as an experiment is infinite (toss a coin forever, pick a point of an interval, follow a particle), because every single outcome then has probability 0.

nodes.title: Probability Spaces and Kolmogorov's Axioms
nodes.essence: A probability space is a triple (Ω, ℱ, P): a set Ω of outcomes, a σ-algebra ℱ of subsets of Ω called events, and a measure P on ℱ with P(Ω) = 1.

nodes.title: Random Variables and Distributions
nodes.essence: A random variable is a measurable function X : Ω → ℝ, a number whose value depends on the outcome ω.

nodes.title: Independence and Zero–One Laws
nodes.essence: Independence is the notion that probability adds to measure theory. Events A and B are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B); random variables are independent when the σ-algebras they generate are, and an infinite family is independent when every finite subfamily is.

nodes.title: Conditional Expectation
nodes.essence: Elementary probability conditions on an event B of positive probability: P(A ∣ B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). That fails exactly where it is most needed, when conditioning on the value of a continuous random variable Z, because {Z = z} has probability 0.

nodes.title: Limit Theorems
nodes.essence: A single random outcome is unpredictable; the sum of many independent ones is not. This area makes that precise for Sₙ = X₁ + … + Xₙ, a sum of n independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) terms with mean μ and variance σ², by describing it at successive scales:

nodes.title: Modes of Convergence
nodes.essence: A sequence of random variables can converge in at least four inequivalent senses, and each limit theorem of probability is a statement in a specific one: the strong law of large numbers is almost sure convergence, the weak law is convergence in probability, the central limit theorem is convergence in distribution.

nodes.title: The Law of Large Numbers
nodes.essence: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables with mean μ = E[X₁], and let X̄ₙ = (X₁ + … + Xₙ)/n be the average of the first n. The law of large numbers says that X̄ₙ → μ: in probability (the weak law) and almost surely (the strong law).

nodes.title: The Central Limit Theorem
nodes.essence: The law of large numbers says that the average of n independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) observations tends to their mean μ; the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) says how it fluctuates on the way.

nodes.title: Concentration Inequalities
nodes.essence: The law of large numbers says that an average approaches its mean; the central limit theorem says how it fluctuates in the limit. Neither says how unlikely a deviation of a given size is at a fixed sample size n, and that is what algorithms, statistics and learning theory need.

nodes.title: Stochastic Processes
nodes.essence: A stochastic process is a family of random variables indexed by time: a random walk, a queue, a stock price, a diffusing particle. The limit theorems study sums of independent terms; processes allow dependence, but of controlled kinds.

nodes.title: Markov Chains
nodes.essence: A Markov chain is a random process whose future depends on the past only through the present: the next state is drawn from a distribution that depends only on the current one.

nodes.title: Martingales
nodes.essence: A martingale is the mathematical model of a fair game: a process whose expected next value, given everything known so far, is its present value.

nodes.title: Brownian Motion
nodes.essence: Brownian motion is the random continuous path that a random walk becomes when its steps are made small and fast in the right proportion.

nodes.title: Stochastic Calculus
nodes.essence: To model a quantity driven by noise, one wants to write dXₜ = b(Xₜ)·dt + σ(Xₜ)·dBₜ, a stochastic differential equation (SDE), where B is Brownian motion. But Brownian paths have no derivative and infinite length, so ∫ H·dB cannot be a Riemann–Stieltjes integral.

nodes.title: Poisson Processes and Continuous-Time Markov Chains
nodes.essence: Many systems change at random instants rather than on the ticks of a clock: atoms decay, customers join a queue, molecules react.

nodes.title: Statistical Inference
nodes.essence: Probability starts from a known distribution and predicts data; statistics starts from data and infers the distribution.

nodes.title: Estimation and Likelihood
nodes.essence: Probability goes from a known distribution to data; statistics goes back. A statistical model is a family of distributions P_θ indexed by a parameter θ, and an estimator is any function of the data used to guess θ.

nodes.title: Hypothesis Tests and Confidence Intervals
nodes.essence: A hypothesis test is a rule for deciding, from data, whether to reject a null hypothesis H₀ in favour of an alternative H₁, designed so that the probability of wrongly rejecting a true H₀ is at most a chosen level α.

nodes.title: Bayesian Inference
nodes.essence: Bayesian inference treats the unknown parameter θ as a random variable.

nodes.title: Linear Models and Regression
nodes.essence: The linear model explains a response by a weighted sum of predictors plus noise: Y = Xβ + ε, where Y is a vector of n observations, X an n × p matrix of known predictors, β an unknown vector of p coefficients and ε random errors with mean 0.

nodes.title: Nonparametric Statistics and the Bootstrap
nodes.essence: Parametric inference assumes a family indexed by a few numbers, such as the normal distributions, and is only as good as that assumption. Nonparametric statistics drops it and lets the data speak about the whole distribution. Three ideas carry the field.

nodes.title: Number Theory and Algebraic Geometry
nodes.essence: Number theory asks about the integers: which equations have integer solutions, how the primes are distributed, which numbers are sums of squares.

nodes.title: Algebraic Number Theory
nodes.essence: Many questions about ordinary integers become easier in a larger ring. Which primes are sums of two squares? Work in ℤ[i], where p = x² + y² means p = (x + iy)(x − iy). Does xᵖ + yᵖ = zᵖ have solutions? Factor the left side over ℤ[ζ_p].

nodes.title: Number Fields and Algebraic Integers
nodes.essence: A number field is a finite extension K of ℚ, such as ℚ(i) or ℚ(√−5). Inside it sits the ring of integers 𝒪_K, the analogue of ℤ: the elements that satisfy a monic polynomial with integer coefficients.

nodes.title: Ideals and the Class Group
nodes.essence: When numbers stop factoring uniquely, pass from numbers to ideals. In the ring of integers 𝒪_K of a number field, every non-zero ideal is a product of prime ideals in exactly one way, because 𝒪_K is a Dedekind domain.

nodes.title: p-adic Numbers and Local Fields
nodes.essence: The real numbers complete ℚ for the usual distance, but ℚ has one other kind of distance for each prime p, in which a number is small when it is divisible by a high power of p.

nodes.title: Class Field Theory
nodes.essence: Galois theory matches the extensions of a field with subgroups of a Galois group, but it does not say what the extensions of ℚ, or of a number field K, actually are.

nodes.title: Analytic Number Theory
nodes.essence: Euclid proved that there are infinitely many primes; analytic number theory asks how many, how they are spread out, and in which patterns they occur. The method is to encode arithmetic in functions and study those functions with analysis.

nodes.title: The Riemann Zeta Function
nodes.essence: The zeta function ζ(s) = ∑ 1/nˢ packages all the integers into one function, and Euler's product formula shows that it packages all the primes too.

nodes.title: The Prime Number Theorem
nodes.essence: The Prime Number Theorem (PNT) says that the number π(x) of primes up to x satisfies π(x) ∼ x/log x: near x, about one integer in log x is prime.

nodes.title: Primes in Arithmetic Progressions
nodes.essence: Dirichlet proved in 1837 that if a and q have greatest common divisor (gcd) 1, then infinitely many primes are congruent to a mod q. His method created analytic number theory.

nodes.title: Sieves and Additive Problems
nodes.essence: Zeta functions count all primes; many questions ask about primes with a twist. Are there infinitely many twin primes p, p + 2? Is every even number above 2 a sum of two primes (Goldbach)? Two tools attack such problems.

nodes.title: Algebraic Geometry
nodes.essence: Algebraic geometry studies the solution sets of polynomial equations as geometric objects.

nodes.title: Varieties and the Nullstellensatz
nodes.essence: Algebraic geometry studies the shapes cut out by polynomial equations: circles, parabolas, surfaces, and their analogues in any number of variables and over any field. Its first discovery is that such a shape and the algebra of polynomials that vanish on it determine each other.

nodes.title: Projective Varieties and Bézout's Theorem
nodes.essence: Two distinct lines in the plane meet in one point, unless they are parallel. A line meets a circle in two points, unless it misses it or touches it.

nodes.title: Algebraic Curves and Riemann–Roch
nodes.essence: A smooth projective curve over ℂ is the same thing as a compact Riemann surface, so it has a topological invariant, the genus g, its number of holes.

nodes.title: Schemes
nodes.essence: The Nullstellensatz matches varieties with certain rings: finitely generated, over an algebraically closed field, with no nilpotents. Grothendieck, around 1960, removed every one of those conditions.

nodes.title: Elliptic Curves and Modular Forms
nodes.essence: This area is where the three earlier ones meet. An elliptic curve is a geometric object, a cubic curve of genus 1, whose rational points form a group studied with the tools of algebraic number theory.

nodes.title: Elliptic Curves
nodes.essence: An elliptic curve is a smooth cubic curve with a chosen point, such as y² = x³ − 2.

nodes.title: Modular Forms
nodes.essence: A modular form is a holomorphic function on the upper half-plane with an enormous amount of symmetry: it transforms in a prescribed way under the group SL₂(ℤ), or one of its subgroups, acting by Möbius transformations.

nodes.title: Fermat's Last Theorem
nodes.essence: Fermat's Last Theorem (FLT) states that xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ has no solutions in positive integers when n ≥ 3. Fermat wrote it in a margin around 1637, claiming a proof that the margin could not contain; it took until 1994. The proof does not attack the equation directly.

nodes.title: The Langlands Programme
nodes.essence: The Langlands programme is a web of conjectures, proposed by Robert Langlands from 1967, that predicts a dictionary between two worlds. On one side are Galois representations, which encode how primes split in number fields and how many points varieties have mod p.

nodes.title: Structure and Metamathematics
nodes.essence: The earlier layers built mathematics: numbers, algebra, spaces, analysis. This layer steps back and makes mathematics itself the object of study, in two ways. The first looks at the structures mathematicians use.

nodes.title: Category Theory
nodes.essence: Every earlier layer studied some kind of structure together with the maps that preserve it: groups and homomorphisms, vector spaces and linear maps, spaces and continuous maps. Category theory takes that pattern as the object of study.

nodes.title: Categories and Functors
nodes.essence: Groups with homomorphisms, vector spaces with linear maps and spaces with continuous maps share one pattern: objects, structure-preserving maps and composition. A category is that pattern made into a definition, and a functor is a map between categories that preserves it.

nodes.title: Natural Transformations and the Yoneda Lemma
nodes.essence: A natural transformation is a map between two functors that is compatible with every arrow. It makes precise the old intuition that some isomorphisms are canonical while others depend on a choice, and with natural transformations as arrows, functors themselves form categories.

nodes.title: Universal Properties and Adjunctions
nodes.essence: Products, quotients, free groups and tensor products were each built by hand in earlier layers, from pairs, equivalence classes, words and formal sums. Each is better defined by what it does: it is the object through which every map of a certain kind factors uniquely.

nodes.title: Homological Algebra
nodes.essence: Simplicial homology of a space and de Rham cohomology of a manifold both come from a sequence of abelian groups with maps whose composite is zero, and both measure how far "boundary" falls short of "cycle".

nodes.title: Higher Categories and Homotopy Type Theory
nodes.essence: In topology two paths are rarely equal, only homotopic, and two homotopies are themselves related by higher homotopies.

nodes.title: Computability and Incompleteness
nodes.essence: In 1900 Hilbert asked for an algorithm to decide whether a Diophantine equation has integer solutions, and in the 1920s he hoped to show that mathematics is complete, consistent and decidable by finitary means.

nodes.title: Computable Functions and the Church–Turing Thesis
nodes.essence: Before one can prove that no algorithm solves a problem, "algorithm" needs a mathematical definition.

nodes.title: Undecidable Problems
nodes.essence: A problem is a family of yes-or-no questions, and it is decidable if one program answers all of them correctly. With computability defined, some families can be proved to have no such program.

nodes.title: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems
nodes.essence: In 1931 Kurt Gödel proved that no consistent, effectively axiomatised theory that contains a modest amount of arithmetic can decide every arithmetical sentence, and that such a theory cannot prove its own consistency.

nodes.title: Proof Theory and Reverse Mathematics
nodes.essence: After Gödel, the useful question is no longer whether a theory proves its own consistency but how strong a theory must be to prove a given theorem.

nodes.title: Computational Complexity
nodes.essence: Computability asks whether a problem can be solved by an algorithm at all; complexity asks what the solution costs, as a function of the input's length. The robust dividing line is polynomial time, the class P.

nodes.title: Model Theory and Independence
nodes.essence: A theory is a set of sentences; a model is a structure in which they are true. Layer 00 showed that the two sides match: a sentence follows from a theory if and only if it holds in every model. Model theory exploits this match in both directions.

nodes.title: Models and the Löwenheim–Skolem Theorems
nodes.essence: Layer 00 proved that first-order logic is complete and compact. Model theory studies the structures that satisfy a theory, and its first lesson is that first-order theories cannot control the size of their models.

nodes.title: Quantifier Elimination and Decidable Theories
nodes.essence: Gödel's theorems say arithmetic with addition and multiplication is undecidable, but many important theories are not: the first-order theory of the real numbers, of the complex numbers, and of the natural numbers with addition alone can all be decided by an algorithm.

nodes.title: Forcing and Independence
nodes.essence: Cantor's continuum hypothesis (CH), that every infinite set of reals is either countable or the size of ℝ, was the first of Hilbert's 1900 problems. It is neither provable nor refutable in Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice (ZFC), if ZFC is consistent.

nodes.title: Large Cardinals
nodes.essence: A large cardinal is an infinite cardinal so big that its existence cannot be proved in Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with choice (ZFC), usually because a set of that size would contain a model of ZFC.

nodes.title: Applied and Computational Mathematics
nodes.essence: This layer asks how mathematics computes, decides and models the world. The rest of the stack proves that objects exist and have properties: a solution to a differential equation, a minimum of a convex function, a code meeting a bound. Here the questions become operational.

nodes.title: Numerical Analysis
nodes.essence: Lloyd Trefethen defined numerical analysis as the study of algorithms for the problems of continuous mathematics.

nodes.title: Floating Point, Conditioning and Stability
nodes.essence: A computer cannot hold a real number. It holds the nearest member of a finite set of binary fractions, and it rounds the exact result of every operation back into that set. Numerical analysis makes this a theory with two separate questions.

nodes.title: Numerical Linear Algebra
nodes.essence: At its core, most scientific computing solves linear systems Ax = b, fits least squares or finds eigenvalues.

nodes.title: Root-Finding and Newton's Method
nodes.essence: Most equations f(x) = 0 have no formula for their solutions, so we guess and improve. Most methods are iterations x_(n+1) = g(xₙ) built so that the root is a fixed point of g, and the questions are always the same: does it converge, from where, and how fast?

nodes.title: Interpolation and Approximation
nodes.essence: To compute with a function you must replace it by something finite, usually a polynomial or piecewise polynomial. Interpolation matches the function exactly at chosen nodes; approximation asks only to be uniformly close.

nodes.title: Numerical Methods for Differential Equations
nodes.essence: A computer cannot follow a continuous trajectory; it takes steps.

nodes.title: Monte Carlo Methods
nodes.essence: Monte Carlo methods compute a number by writing it as an expectation and averaging random samples.

nodes.title: The Fast Fourier Transform and Spectral Methods
nodes.essence: The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) turns n samples of a signal into n frequency coefficients. Done directly it costs n² operations; the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) needs O(n log n), which made Fourier analysis a routine computation. Two consequences dominate.

nodes.title: Optimisation
nodes.essence: Optimisation chooses the best point of a set: minimise f(x) subject to constraints.

nodes.title: Linear Programming
nodes.essence: A linear programme asks for the maximum of a linear function cᵀx subject to linear inequalities Ax ≤ b. The feasible set is a polyhedron, and a bounded optimum is always attained at a vertex, so the problem is combinatorial in disguise: which constraints are tight?

nodes.title: Convex Optimisation and Duality
nodes.essence: A convex optimisation problem minimises a convex function over a convex set, typically given by convex inequalities fᵢ(x) ≤ 0 and affine equations. R.

nodes.title: Gradient Methods
nodes.essence: Gradient descent repeats one step: move against the gradient, xₖ₊₁ = xₖ − η∇f(xₖ). Each step costs one gradient and no matrix factorisation, so the method scales to problems with billions of variables where Newton's method cannot even store the Hessian.

nodes.title: Information, Codes and Cryptography
nodes.essence: This area is the mathematics of sending messages. Three adversaries stand between sender and receiver: redundancy, which wastes bandwidth; noise, which corrupts symbols; and eavesdroppers, who read or alter what is sent.

nodes.title: Information Theory
nodes.essence: Claude Shannon's paper "A Mathematical Theory of Communication" (1948) created a subject complete with its main theorems. It measures information by entropy, the average number of bits needed to describe the outcome of a random source, and proves two limits.

nodes.title: Error-Correcting Codes
nodes.essence: An error-correcting code adds redundancy to a message so that the receiver can recover it even after some symbols are corrupted. Shannon's theorem promises codes that approach channel capacity but does not say how to build or decode them.

nodes.title: Cryptography
nodes.essence: Cryptography makes communication secure against an adversary. Its mathematical turn came in two steps. Claude Shannon (1949) defined perfect secrecy and showed it needs a key as long as the message.

nodes.title: Mathematical Modelling
nodes.essence: A model maps a piece of the world to a mathematical object whose consequences can be computed and compared with measurement. This area asks how a physical, biological or engineered system is turned into equations, and what can be trusted about the answer.

nodes.title: Modelling and Dimensional Analysis
nodes.essence: A mathematical model replaces a system by equations whose solutions can be compared with measurement. Modelling is a cycle: idealise, write down the laws, simplify by scaling, solve, test against data the model was not built from, and revise.

nodes.title: Control Theory
nodes.essence: Control theory asks how to choose the inputs to a dynamical system so that it behaves as intended despite disturbances and model error. Its central idea is feedback: measure the output, compare it with the goal, and let the difference drive the input.

nodes.title: Mathematical Biology and Epidemics
nodes.essence: Mathematical biology writes populations, infections and tissues as dynamical systems and asks which qualitative behaviours the mechanisms force: saturation, oscillation, outbreak or pattern.

nodes.title: The Mathematics of Quantum Mechanics
nodes.essence: Quantum mechanics is a probability theory whose events are closed subspaces of a complex Hilbert space rather than subsets of a sample space.

nodes.title: The Geometry of General Relativity
nodes.essence: General relativity, completed by Albert Einstein in November 1915, says that gravity is not a force but the curvature of spacetime.

nodes.title: Games, Decisions and Finance
nodes.essence: Most of applied mathematics models systems that do not care about the outcome. This area models agents who do: players choosing strategies, voters ranking candidates, traders pricing risk.

nodes.title: Game Theory
nodes.essence: Game theory studies decisions whose outcome depends on what others decide. A game lists players, their strategies and their payoffs, and the basic question is what rational players will do when each knows the others are also reasoning. Two theorems anchor the subject.

nodes.title: Social Choice and Voting
nodes.essence: Social choice theory asks how individual preferences should be combined into a collective decision. Each voter ranks the alternatives, and a rule must turn the list of rankings into a social ranking or a winner.

nodes.title: Mathematical Finance
nodes.essence: Mathematical finance prices contracts whose payoff depends on an uncertain future, such as an option to buy a share at a fixed price later. Its founding principle is no arbitrage: in a sensible market no trading strategy turns nothing into a riskless profit.

nodes.title: Data and Learning
nodes.essence: This area asks when a finite amount of data determines something that is in principle infinite: a function from a few labelled examples, a signal from a few measurements, a structure from a cloud of points in a thousand dimensions.

nodes.title: Statistical Learning Theory
nodes.essence: Statistical learning theory asks when a rule fitted to finitely many examples will work on new ones. Data are drawn independently from an unknown distribution, a learner picks a hypothesis from a class H, and success means low error on fresh draws, not on the sample.

nodes.title: High-Dimensional Geometry and Random Matrices
nodes.essence: Data often live in thousands of dimensions, where planar intuition fails. Almost all the volume of a ball lies in a thin shell near its surface, two random directions are almost perpendicular, and any reasonable function of many independent variables is almost constant.

nodes.title: Sampling and Compressed Sensing
nodes.essence: A continuous signal has infinitely many values, yet a digital device stores only finitely many samples. The sampling theorem says when nothing is lost: a signal containing no frequencies above B is determined by its values at 2B equally spaced points per second.

nodes.title: The Mathematics of Deep Learning
nodes.essence: A neural network is a composition of simple maps: f(x) = W_L σ(⋯ σ(W₁x + b₁) ⋯) + b_L, where the W's are matrices, the b's vectors and σ a fixed nonlinear function applied coordinate by coordinate. Training fits billions of parameters to data by gradient descent.

nodes.title: Optimal Transport
nodes.essence: Optimal transport asks for the cheapest way to move one distribution of mass onto another, when moving a unit of mass from x to y costs c(x, y).

nodes.title: Mathematics in Context
nodes.essence: Every layer below states definitions, theorems and proofs.

nodes.title: History of Mathematics
nodes.essence: Mathematics began as calculation for practical ends and became, in Greece, a deductive science in which results follow from stated assumptions by proof.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Mathematics
nodes.essence: Philosophy of mathematics asks what mathematical statements are about, how we know them, and why they apply to the physical world. Mathematical objects are not seen or touched, yet theorems about them seem more certain than any empirical law.

nodes.title: Mathematical Practice and Discovery
nodes.essence: Published mathematics looks like a chain of definitions, lemmas and proofs, but that is the finished product, not the process.

nodes.title: Computers and Proof
nodes.essence: Computers entered mathematical proof in three ways. First, as calculators doing case checks too large for humans, starting with the four colour theorem in 1976.

nodes.title: Open Problems
nodes.essence: Some questions resist every attack for decades or centuries, and naming them organises research: Hilbert's list of 1900 shaped twentieth-century mathematics, and the Clay Mathematics Institute announced seven Millennium Prize Problems on 24 May 2000, each carrying a million-dollar prize.

nodes.title: Learning and Teaching Mathematics
nodes.essence: Mathematics is cumulative: each layer of this knowledge base presupposes the ones below, so a learner who misses a step is blocked later in a way that rarely happens in subjects whose parts are more independent.

nodes.title: Mathematics and Society
nodes.essence: Mathematics shapes society mostly invisibly: number theory secures online payments, linear algebra ranks web pages, relativity corrects satellite navigation, and integral transforms turn X-ray projections into medical images.
